overview: This file documents the development of U.S. policy toward Japanese merchant shipping and shipbuilding during the occupation. It begins with a draft and revised memorandum of a November 1948 meeting between State and Army officials and shipping-industry representative Frazer Bailey, whose organization feared that a large revived Japanese fleet would compete unfairly with American shipping. The later May 1949 policy memorandum weighs security, reparations, economic rehabilitation, interagency jurisdiction, vessel acquisition, access to U.S. ports, and the applicability to Japan of occupation rules already adopted for Germany.

subfiles.title: Saltzman comments on the Japanese shipbuilding memorandum
subfiles.about: Saltzman proposes three revisions to Norton's draft account of the November 16 meeting with Frazer Bailey.
subfiles.summary: Saltzman judges the draft substantially complete and accurate but recommends more precise language on reparations and Japanese economic recovery. He also asks that Bailey's information be attributed to representatives of other countries on the Far Eastern Commission and that the record make clear that no U.S. proposal had created a deadlock over the overall size of Japan's merchant fleet. These changes were incorporated into the final memorandum on pages 5–7.

subfiles.title: Norton cover note requesting Saltzman's comments
subfiles.about: Norton forwards the attached draft memorandum and requests Saltzman's comments.
subfiles.summary: This brief internal cover note asks Saltzman to review the attached account of the November 16 meeting. It documents the circulation and clearance process that produced the revised memorandum.

subfiles.title: Draft memorandum of conversation on Japanese shipbuilding
subfiles.to: Department of State and Department of the Army internal circulation
subfiles.about: A draft record of discussions between U.S. officials and Frazer Bailey concerning Japanese shipbuilding capacity and the future size of Japan's merchant fleet.
subfiles.summary: State and Army officials explain that the immediate issues before the National Security Council and Far Eastern Commission concern removal of shipbuilding facilities as reparations rather than establishment of a fixed merchant-fleet ceiling. Bailey argues that a four-million-ton Japanese fleet would unfairly burden American operators and advocates a fleet of about 2.4 million tons, sufficient for domestic trade and half of Japan's foreign trade. Officials reply that Japan's existing 1.15-million-ton fleet is old, poorly suited to ocean service, and unlikely to become competitive quickly without U.S. steel or financial promotion. Bailey is promised consultation before a decision on fleet size.

subfiles.title: Final memorandum of conversation on Japanese shipbuilding
subfiles.to: Department of State and Department of the Army internal circulation
subfiles.about: The revised official record of the November 16 meeting on U.S. policy toward Japanese merchant shipping and shipbuilding.
subfiles.summary: The final version incorporates Saltzman's revisions, emphasizing that reparations should not remove industrial capacity to the point of obstructing Japan's recovery to a reasonably self-supporting economy. It attributes Bailey's understanding of a supposed four-million-ton U.S. position to comments from representatives of other Far Eastern Commission countries. It also states explicitly that no U.S. representative had advanced a definite recommendation for the overall size of Japan's fleet and therefore no known deadlock existed. The memorandum otherwise preserves Bailey's competition concerns and the officials' assessment that Japan's aging 1.15-million-ton fleet could not expand rapidly.

subfiles.title: Fussell memorandum on TRC policy for Japanese shipping
subfiles.to: J. E. Saugstad and L. F. Nickell
subfiles.about: Fussell reviews the institutional and policy issues affecting a TRC position on Japanese shipbuilding and merchant shipping during the occupation.
subfiles.summary: Fussell surveys the U.S. position against limiting Japan's peaceful industrial capacity, the absence of a specific National Security Council security ruling on shipping, Army support for unrestricted resumption, Navy opinion, Maritime Commission jurisdictional claims, and requests for consultation from shipping and labor organizations. He recommends interagency review and renewed consultation with the National Federation of American Shipping and the C.I.O. Substantively, he proposes using the German occupation settlement as a guide while giving Japan no coastal-shipping priority, retaining comparable vessel size and speed restrictions, and permitting immediate acquisition of a limited ocean-going fleet. He advises handling transfers of U.S. government-owned vessels and access to U.S. ports separately and stresses that occupation-period restrictions should not extend beyond the peace treaty.

interest: The file is especially useful because it preserves both a draft policy record and the editorial correspondence that transformed it into the final version, allowing historians to see how officials refined the language of occupation policy. It also captures the tension between Japan's economic rehabilitation and American commercial fears of renewed Japanese maritime competition. The May 1949 memorandum broadens the picture by showing how State, Army, Navy, the Maritime Commission, organized shipping, and labor competed to influence policy, and how officials used the German occupation regime as a comparative model while recognizing Japan's distinctive dependence on long-distance trade.
